I spent way too much time trying to build the "perfect" product.

Turns out, perfection isn't what moves a project forward. Progress is.

Over the last year, I've worked on everything from building e-commerce websites and managing databases to learning UX design and experimenting with new ideas.

One thing every project has taught me is this:

You rarely get it right on the first try.

A design that felt perfect needed user feedback.

A feature I thought people would love ended up being unnecessary.

A bug that took hours to fix taught me more than an entire tutorial.

Building things has made me appreciate the process more than the outcome.

Every mistake leaves you with a better system, a better product, and a better way of thinking.

Still learning.
Still building.
Still improving.

I think perfection is one of the biggest reasons people never start.

I've fallen into that trap more times than I'd like to admit.

Waiting for the perfect design.
The perfect feature.
The perfect time to launch.

The problem?

While you're chasing perfect, someone else is learning from version 1.

One thing I've learned from building products is that your first version is supposed to be imperfect.

That's the point.

You launch.
You get feedback.
You improve.
You repeat.

No amount of planning will teach you as much as putting something in front of real users.

The products we admire today didn't start where they are now.

They started with a first version that was simply good enough to exist.

So if you're waiting for everything to be perfect before you start, this is your reminder:

Done beats perfect.
Every single time.

One of the hardest lessons I've learned is this:

Users don't see your effort.

They don't know that you spent 10 hours fixing a bug.

They don't know you redesigned the same screen five times.

They don't know how many late nights went into getting a feature ready.

And honestly...

They shouldn't have to.

People remember how a product makes them feel, not how difficult it was to build.

That's changed the way I think about creating things.

Instead of asking, "How much work did this take?"

I try to ask, "Is this easier for the person using it?"

Because at the end of the day, the best products don't make users appreciate the effort behind them.

They make users forget there was ever a problem to solve.

That's what I'm striving to build.

What lesson has building something taught you that surprised you?

approved.post_text:
You rarely notice good design.

But you almost always notice bad design.

A confusing checkout.

A button that doesn't work.

A form that keeps throwing errors.

A door that says "Pull" when you instinctively push.

Those moments stick with us because good design quietly disappears into the background.

When something feels intuitive, we don't stop to appreciate it. We simply get on with what we wanted to do.

And that's exactly the goal.

Good design isn't about making people say, "Wow, this looks amazing."

It's about making sure they never have to stop and think, "What do I do next?"

The more I learn about UX, the more I realize that great design is really about anticipating problems before users ever encounter them.

When you've thought through the edge cases, removed unnecessary friction, and made every interaction feel natural, people won't notice your design.

They'll just notice that everything works.

Ironically, that's one of the biggest compliments a designer can receive.

Do you think the best design is the one users never notice?
